Emotion regulation is a significant area of psychological research that requires investigation of processes that are often difficult for participants to describe, involving implicit and automatic actions. However, research examining emotion regulatory processes often requires individuals to modify their emotional responses in the moment and to report on that strategy use. We aimed to determine if individuals are able to change the regulation of their emotions when implicit goals are made explicit.

Undergraduates ( n = 101) watched four fear-eliciting films. Between the second and third films, participants were provided psychoeducation on emotion regulation and then, after each of the final two films, participants were asked to report on the emotion regulation strategies they used during those films. Differences in self-reported affect, facial expression, and skin conductance were examined between, before, and after the emotion regulation instruction, as well as between the final two films.

Results suggested little difference in emotion response output following emotion regulation education and strategy reports and that individuals higher in trait negative affectivity were least responsive.

Hence, individuals may struggle to respond when implicit regulatory goals become explicit. This has implications for future research, but also for interventions that commonly rely on explicit emotion regulation goals and processes.

Emotion regulation refers to the process by which individuals upregulate or downregulate their emotional experience and responses in the service of goals either deliberately or automatically ( Campos et al., 2004 ; Cole et al., 1994 ; Gross, 2015 ; Koole and Rothermund, 2011 ; Mauss et al., 2007 ). Dominant models, including the Process Model of Emotion Regulation ( Gross, 1998 , 2015 ), typically identify multiple points during emotional contexts in which one can engage in emotion regulation, from prior to the context (e.g., behavioral avoidance of an evocative situation) to shifts in cognition (e.g., reappraisal, acceptance) and attention (e.g., distraction) during and after evocative contexts to modulate emotional experience. Moreover, research over decades has demonstrated that hedonic goals (i.e., reducing discomfort), are most dominant across most individuals and circumstances ( English et al., 2017 ; Larsen, 2000 ; Riediger et al., 2009 ). Deficits in negative emotion regulatory processes are broadly implicated in the development and maintenance of most psychiatric disorders ( Krueger and Eaton, 2015 ; Sloan et al., 2017 ) and thus are increasingly and explicitly targeted in interventions (i.e., Dialectical Behavior Therapy: Linehan, 1993 ; Emotion Regulation Therapy; Fresco et al., 2013 ). Hence, research investigating emotion regulatory processes is widespread, with searches of the term “emotion regulation” on Pub Med spawning thousands of articles. Importantly, efforts to define, understand, and modify emotion regulation have largely focused on self-reported difficulties of emotion regulation, self-reported use of emotion regulation strategies during emotional situations, and investigation of instructed vs. spontaneous emotion regulation efficacy.

In examining explicit and implicit emotion regulation processes, it is important to consider what we mean by explicit and implicit. In Braunstein et al., 2017 , the authors identify an important distinction between emotion regulation goals and emotion regulation change processes. Regulatory goals can be explicit, when the individual’s primary goal is to regulate their emotions and they are aware of this goal, or implicit, referring to times when an individual does not have a conscious desire or goal to regulate their emotions but instead responds based on general hedonic tendencies ( Eldesouky and English, 2018 ).
